facts.text: A 2.6-acre plaza dedicated to commemorate the formation of the United Nations.
Lawrence Halprin designed the large sunken fountain.
Hosts the Heart-of-the-City Farmers Market on Wednesdays and Sundays, held there since 1981.
Built as the U.S. Courthouse and Post Office, with groundbreaking in 1897.
Supervising Architect James Knox Taylor played a lead role in the design.
A steel-framed building clad in white Sierra granite.
Renamed for Judge James R. Browning, who served as a circuit judge for four decades.
One of only two buildings south of Market Street to survive the 1906 earthquake and fires, with the 1874 U.S. Mint.
Consists of a shell-pocked section of the cruiser USS San Francisco's bridge wings.
A plaque honors about 100 sailors and seven Marines who died aboard the cruiser.
Oriented towards Guadalcanal.
Dedicated on March 23, 1914, as a monument to composer Giuseppe Verdi in Golden Gate Park.
Ettore Patrizi, editor of L'Italia, led the subscription fund that raised $15,000 for it.
About 24 feet high and 52 tons, with a base of red and black Baveno granite from Italy.
Restored in 2003, when the bust of Verdi at the top was regilded.
Erected by the San Francisco Art Commission for the Waterfront Transportation Projects.
The marker text says whaling by open boats from San Francisco ended in 1910.
Sculpted by Robert Ingersoll Aitken, as a statue of a female figure representing the Republic.
Theodore Roosevelt broke ground for the monument in Golden Gate Park on May 13, 1903.
Unveiled on November 24, 1904, at the entrance to the Panhandle.
The World War II West Coast Memorial honors servicemen lost or buried at sea in Pacific waters in 1941-1945.
A curved granite wall inscribed with the names of 413 servicemen, dedicated November 29, 1960.
Designed by architects Hervey Parke Clark and John F. Beuttler.
Features a statue of Columbia by French sculptor Jean De Marco.
Opened in 1913 as La Bonita and renamed the Star in 1927.
Renamed the 4 Star in 1946 after new owners took over and upgraded it.
Became an art house offering independent and foreign films.
A 20-seat attraction combining motion seats, a giant 3D screen and laser blasters.
Scenarios include battling zombies, werewolves, demented clowns or road fighters.
Timothy Pflueger remodeled the theater in Art Deco style in 1932 for the Nasser Brothers circuit.
Has a 70-foot marquee sign that is a local landmark.
Closed in 1993 and became a furniture store before Alamo Drafthouse renovated it.
Reopened as a movie theater, restaurant and bar in December 2015, keeping the name New Mission Theater.
Built as the Islam Temple for the Shriners, used for their meetings and ceremonies from 1918 to 1970.
The facade has Byzantine arches and filigree lattice work in polychrome terra cotta.
Designed as a Kabuki theater with a revolving stage and trap doors, serving dinner to the audience.
Was the first multiplex in San Francisco.
Has screened films for the San Francisco International Film Festival and shows San Francisco Opera performances.
Opened June 16, 1999 as Sony Theatres Metreon; later run by Loews Cineplex, then AMC.
Designed by David Rockwell.
Recliner seats were added in 2020, reducing capacity to 1,727.
Opened July 10, 1998 as the AMC 1000 Van Ness multiplex.
Operated as CGV Cinemas San Francisco from September 2021 until it closed in February 2023.
Apple Cinemas took it over in June 2025 and reopened it on July 10, 2025.
A sound art event presented weekly since 1967, with its first public performance on May 26, 1967.
Created by composer Stan Shaff and performed on equipment designed by Doug McEachern.
Works are sculpted in space through 176 speakers in a completely dark theater.
Opened February 27, 1926 with 800 seats, named after Vasco Nunez de Balboa.
Founded by Samuel H. Levin, whose family ran it until February 2001.
Part of the CinemaSFBay chain since 2012.
Began as Bay Area Theatresports after a November 10, 1986 workshop led by Rebecca Stockley.
Took up permanent residency at the Bayfront Theater in Fort Mason Center in 1997.
Renamed BATS Improv in 2001.

name: Bayview Opera House Ruth Williams Memorial Theatre

facts.text: Built by the Masons, and described as the oldest standing theater in San Francisco.
Operated by the nonprofit Bayview Opera House, Inc., which provides arts education for youth.
A $5.7 million renovation led by the Arts Commission added a plaza with a wooden stage.
Operated by Another Planet Entertainment, which hosts over 100 concerts and events a year.
Joseph Kosuth's neon work W.F.T. (San Francisco) is on the exterior of the western side.

name: Blue Shield of California Theater at YBCA

facts.text: A proscenium theater with two-tier seating and 757 seats.
Designed by architects James Stewart Polshek and Todd Schliemann.
An 18-hole mini golf course themed on the West's story of boom and bust.
Built by the Bayview fabrication shop One Hat One Hand, with 150 local artists.
Includes a replica of Chinatown's Dragon Gate and a recreated Gold Rush-era saloon.
Brava for Women in the Arts bought the shuttered York Theater, built in 1926, and renamed it in 1996.
A $3 million renovation created a 360-seat main theater and a 60-seat studio.
Run by Brava for Women in the Arts, founded in 1986 by Ellen Gavin with 75 women artists.
Created in a renovated historic grand ballroom in the Ann Getty Center for Education.
Seats an audience of 348.
A performance venue with 224 retractable seats and a full performance stage.

name: CinéArts at the Empire
note: Closed permanently in January 2021; 2026 results discuss demolition for housing.
